text: In course twelve, a code commit triggered a pipeline: run tests, and if they pass, build, deploy, and reconcile automatically with GitOps. MLOps CI/CD is the exact same shape with a different artifact at the center — a model instead of a binary. The commit, the tests, and the deployment all have direct model equivalents, and that's what this lesson walks through.

The trigger isn't always a code push anymore. It can be new data simply accumulating on a schedule, a drift alert from the monitoring system firing the pipeline directly, or a change to the training script or hyperparameters, committed the same way application code is. The tests become the evaluation gate from lesson seventeen, and deployment becomes a registry promotion instead of a container rollout.

In a real pipeline definition, all three triggers sit side by side — a weekly cron schedule, a repository dispatch event fired by the monitoring system, and a push trigger watching the training code path. Whichever one fires, the same two steps run: train the model, then evaluate it against the current production baseline before anything is allowed to move forward.

That evaluation step is the heart of the whole pattern. Instead of a person staring at a dashboard deciding whether a number looks good, the pipeline itself pulls the current production model's metrics straight from the registry and compares them against the new model. If the new model doesn't clear that bar, the pipeline exits with a failure — and that failure is the system working exactly as designed, not a bug to chase down.

When a retrained model does clear the gate, the pipeline's last step promotes it in the registry automatically, calling the same stage-transition function from lesson eighteen — no person needs to type a promotion command. That's GitOps applied to a model: the desired production version is declared through an automated, passing pipeline run, not a manual change typed against a live system.

You've now seen two of the three retraining triggers in action — scheduled runs and code changes. The third, a drift alert, is the one that actually detects when a model needs retraining in the first place, and that's exactly what lesson twenty covers next: how model monitoring spots drift in production before accuracy quietly falls apart.
